title: Dunkirk: How 338,000 Men Escaped a Trap
alt_titles: Dunkirk: The Rescue That Saved Britain's Army
Operation Dynamo: Nine Days at Dunkirk
Why Did Hitler's Tanks Stop at Dunkirk?
description_summary: In May 1940, the British army and its allies were trapped against the sea at Dunkirk. Planners hoped to save 45,000 men; in nine days, more than 338,000 got away. This is the story of the halt order, the East Mole, the little ships and the rearguard that made it possible.

sources.title: Ramsay's despatch on Operation Dynamo, London Gazette

scenes.narration: By 27 May 1940, British and French soldiers were crowding onto the beaches around Dunkirk, in northern France. Behind them, German forces were closing in. In front of them lay the open sea, and there were almost no boats to take them off. German aircraft were already bombing the town and its harbour. On that first full day of the rescue, just 7,669 men got away.

stick.label: May 1940: the retreat to the coast

scenes.narration: Britain's leaders hoped to save around 45,000 men before the Germans broke through. Nine days later, more than 338,000 had been brought out. This is the story of how it happened. It involves a German order still argued over, a harbour wall never built for ships, and hundreds of civilian boats.

shots.caption: Troops on the beach at Dunkirk, late May 1940

shots.file: File:Troops evacuated from Dunkirk on a destroyer about to berth at Dover, 31 May 1940. H1637.jpg
shots.caption: Rescued troops on a destroyer arriving at Dover, 31 May 1940

scenes.narration: On 10 May 1940, Germany invaded the Netherlands, Belgium and France. Its armoured divisions pushed through the Ardennes forest, which the Allies had thought too difficult for tanks. On 20 May, they reached the English Channel. The best Allied armies in the north were cut off.

shots.caption: The German advance, 21 May to 4 June 1940
The fighting in Belgium, 16 to 21 May 1940

scenes.narration: Trapped among them was the British Expeditionary Force, commanded by General Lord Gort. On 19 May, Gort began to consider escape by sea. Within days, Dunkirk was the last port still open to the British. Retreating units abandoned their lorries and marched for the coast.

shots.file: File:John Gort at Arras WWII IWM O 177.jpg
shots.caption: General Lord Gort, commander of the British Expeditionary Force

shots.file: File:The British Expeditionary Force (BEF) in France 1939-1940 F4629.jpg
shots.caption: British troops in France, 1939 to 1940

scenes.narration: Then the German tanks stopped. Late on 23 May, General Gerd von Rundstedt ordered his armour to halt. Hitler visited his headquarters the next day and confirmed the order. The tanks waited for around two days, just a few miles from Dunkirk. Those days gave the Allies time to build a defence line.

Why the tanks halted is still debated. Commanders worried about losing tanks needed for the rest of France. Hermann Göring promised that his air force could destroy the trapped armies alone. Some later claimed Hitler wanted to spare Britain. Most historians reject that idea.

The rescue was run from tunnels beneath Dover Castle by Vice Admiral Bertram Ramsay. The Admiralty ordered it to begin at 6.57 in the evening on Sunday 26 May. It was called Operation Dynamo. The plan aimed to lift up to 45,000 men within two days. After that, Ramsay's staff expected German attacks to end the operation.

shots.caption: Admiral Bertram Ramsay, who ran the rescue

card.label: men the plan hoped to save

scenes.narration: The first days were slow. The beaches sloped so gently that large ships could not get close. Soldiers waded out to small boats, which then ferried them to the ships waiting offshore. The shortest crossing ran within range of German guns on the coast, so many ships took longer routes. In the first two days, only about 25,000 men escaped.

shots.caption: Troops at Dunkirk, 1940

card.label: escaped in the first two days

shots.caption: The three sea routes used during the evacuation

scenes.narration: The man in charge on the spot, Captain William Tennant, looked for a faster way. Dunkirk harbour had a long breakwater called the East Mole. It was never meant for ships to tie up against. Tennant decided to try it anyway.

shots.caption: The East Mole at Dunkirk

scenes.narration: It worked. Ships moored against the narrow walkway, and long lines of soldiers filed along it to board. Almost 200,000 men would leave from the moles, far more than from the beaches. Each night, the queue along the Mole stretched back towards the town.

shots.file: File:Fenella at the East Mole, Dunkirk..jpeg
shots.caption: The ship Fenella at the East Mole

scenes.narration: To fetch men from the beaches, the navy needed boats that could work in shallow water. On 27 May, officials began calling boatyards to collect them. Some owners agreed to hand their boats over. Others found them taken before anyone could ask.

shots.caption: Small craft at Dunkirk, 1940

scenes.narration: Over 800 vessels took part in the evacuation. They included destroyers, ferries, fishing boats, pleasure steamers and private motor yachts. Many of the smallest were crewed by naval personnel, but some went with their owners. By 31 May, nearly 400 small craft were working off the coast.

shots.file: File:The Withdrawal from Dunkirk, June 1940 Art.IWMARTLD305.jpg
shots.caption: The Withdrawal from Dunkirk, painted by Charles Cundall, 1940

scenes.narration: Some became famous. Tamzine, a fishing boat under fifteen feet long, was the smallest known boat in the evacuation. It is now kept at the Imperial War Museum. The paddle steamer Medway Queen made seven round trips. She is credited with rescuing about 7,000 men.

shots.caption: Tamzine, the smallest known Dunkirk boat

card.label: made by the paddle steamer Medway Queen

scenes.narration: One owner was 66 year old Charles Lightoller, the most senior officer to survive the sinking of the Titanic. He had also commanded a destroyer in the First World War. On 1 June, he took his motor yacht Sundowner to Dunkirk with his son Roger and a Sea Scout, Gerald Ashcroft. They brought back around 130 men, packed into every space aboard. Sundowner still survives, and is kept at Ramsgate in Kent.

shots.caption: Charles Lightoller, Titanic's most senior surviving officer

scenes.narration: The rescue went on under constant attack. German aircraft bombed the harbour, the beaches and the ships. The weather sometimes helped. On 30 May, low cloud kept most German planes away. On clear days, losses at sea mounted quickly.

shots.caption: Dunkirk under attack, 1940

scenes.narration: Six British destroyers were sunk and nineteen damaged. The French lost three destroyers. In the air, the RAF lost 145 aircraft and the Luftwaffe 156. Many soldiers on the beaches complained that they never saw the RAF, because much of the fighting happened inland or above the clouds.

As the system improved, the numbers rose sharply. On 31 May, 68,014 men were brought out, the highest total of any single day. That evening, Lord Gort left for England, as ordered. Command of the British troops still ashore passed to General Harold Alexander.

shots.file: File:Wounded British soldiers evacuated from Dunkirk make their way up the gangplank from a destroyer at Dover, 31 May 1940. H1623.jpg
shots.caption: Wounded soldiers come ashore at Dover, 31 May 1940

scenes.narration: The escape depended on soldiers who stayed behind. Near Lille, the French First Army fought on from 28 to 31 May. It held off seven German divisions that could otherwise have pressed towards Dunkirk. When it surrendered, tens of thousands of French soldiers were taken prisoner.

card.label: German divisions held off at Lille

scenes.narration: Around Dunkirk itself, French and British troops held the perimeter while the ships came and went. In the final days, the rescue worked mostly at night. More than 100,000 French soldiers were brought out. Many of them were shipped back to France within days to keep fighting. Operation Dynamo ended on 4 June, and the town fell the same day.

In all, 338,226 Allied soldiers were rescued. About 198,000 were British, and about 140,000 were French and Belgian. That was more than seven times the 45,000 the planners had hoped for. It was far beyond anything thought possible a week before.

shots.file: File:The British Army in the United Kingdom- Evacuation From Dunkirk, May-June 1940 H1690.jpg
shots.caption: Evacuated troops back in Britain, 1940

scenes.narration: But the army had come home almost empty handed. It left behind 2,472 artillery guns and nearly 65,000 other vehicles. It also lost 20,000 motorcycles and almost all of the 445 British tanks sent to France. Rebuilding that equipment would take years. At home, volunteers met the trains carrying returning soldiers with tea and food.

shots.file: File:The British Evacuation From Dunkirk in 1940 HU2286.jpg
shots.caption: Abandoned equipment near Dunkirk, 1940

scenes.narration: The human cost was heavy too. During the campaign from 10 May to 22 June, the British Expeditionary Force suffered 68,000 casualties. That figure includes killed, wounded and captured. Many of those captured spent the next five years as prisoners of war.

shots.file: File:Dunkirk and the Retreat From France 1940 HU104600.jpg
shots.caption: The retreat from France, 1940

scenes.narration: On 4 June, Winston Churchill reported to the House of Commons. He had been prime minister for less than four weeks. A week earlier, he had told MPs to prepare for hard and heavy tidings. Now he could report something better. He called the rescue a miracle of deliverance. But he warned against calling it a victory. Wars, he said, are not won by evacuations.

shots.file: File:Winston Churchill As Prime Minister 1940-1945 H2646A.jpg
shots.caption: Winston Churchill, prime minister from May 1940

card.text: Wars are not won by evacuations.

scenes.narration: He called the campaign a colossal military disaster. Yet the same speech ended with a promise to keep fighting. Britain, he said, would fight on the beaches, on the landing grounds, in the fields and in the streets, and would never surrender. That evening, a BBC announcer read parts of the speech on the radio. Churchill did not broadcast it himself. France signed an armistice with Germany on 22 June.

card.text: We shall fight on the beaches.

scenes.narration: Dunkirk mattered because it kept Britain's army alive. The men rescued became the core of the forces that fought on. The phrase Dunkirk spirit entered the language. And Bertram Ramsay went on to plan the naval side of the D-Day landings in 1944, taking the army back across the Channel.

shots.caption: Ramsay's statue at Dover Castle

scenes.narration: It was a defeat that became a rescue, and a rescue that made it possible to fight on. It rested on a pause no one fully understands, a breakwater, a rearguard and hundreds of boats. Sources and image credits are in the description.
